asDecan.p: Each sign is cut into three ten-degree slices called decans, and each slice gets a planet and one of the small cards. Your Sun sits in the first ten degrees of Aries, which in the old Golden Dawn order belong to Mars. Mars already rules Aries, so here the sign's own planet runs the sign's own opening stretch. It's also where the zodiac begins, and Aries is cardinal fire, a sign that opens a season. The next slice along goes to the Sun, the Three of Wands, which is warmer and a bit keener to be seen. The last is Venus, the Four, which likes company and a finished house. Yours has neither of those softeners. The Emperor is your card for Aries as a whole, and the Two of Wands narrows that down to your few degrees. Have a look at the man on the castle wall, one wand fixed to the stone, a small globe in his hand. For a Mars card he's standing surprisingly still.

You usually know what you want before you know why, and you've gone for it before the why turns up. In a meeting where everyone's circling the problem, you're the one who says 'right, so who's doing what', and half the room is relieved and the other half is a bit put out. A friendly game of cards at Christmas stops being friendly about ten minutes after you sit down. A group chat trying to pick a weekend away can go on for days, and by the second evening you've lost patience and booked the place. A free Saturday is fine until mid-morning, then you're out the back pulling up the old pavers. A queue that isn't moving, you feel that in your legs. With Mars running its own sign there's very little gap between wanting a thing and doing it.

The gift people don't expect is how clean you are to deal with. There's no second version of you keeping score in the background. If something's bothering you, you say so, usually the same day, and the people who work with you learn they never have to guess where they stand. That's rarer than it sounds, and a lot of colleagues find it a relief after years of reading between the lines. The other thing is how you take a no. Mars at home doesn't sit in a loss for long. A pitch gets knocked back or a date never texts, and you feel it hard for one evening. I've seen an early Aries Sun get passed over for a promotion on a Friday and be halfway through a business plan by Monday lunchtime.

The less obvious trouble is that your courage is mostly the doing kind. Give you a fire to put out or a bully to stand up to and you're first in. Give you something that can't be fixed by moving, a friend who's grieving and just needs you on the couch with them, a sister who wants to talk the same problem through for the third time, and you get fidgety and start offering solutions nobody asked for. Sometimes you'll pick a fight because a fight is at least something to do. The other habit is always being half into the next thing, so the people who've been there all along start to feel like part of the furniture. Your mum or your oldest mate can go three months without hearing from you, and you honestly didn't notice the time go.

When something goes wrong your first move is to do something, fast. Someone you love ends up in hospital and within the hour you've sorted the lifts, the dog and who's bringing food. A breakup, and you're at the gym at six the next morning going much too hard. That first burst is useful and gets real things done. A week on it's usually turned into irritability. You're short with whoever's at home, you swear at the driver in front, and you sleep badly because your body's been revved up for days with nowhere to go. The people near you get the heat without the explanation, which isn't fair on them. What actually helps is something physical and hard enough to burn off the Mars, a long run, a cold swim, splitting wood, and then one person you'll let see you sad once the anger's gone.

Libra sits opposite Aries, and you're often drawn to people who are good at exactly the things you skip. The ones who ask how everyone's feeling, who take a week to decide on a couch, who notice the tone of a message. It can drive you up the wall, and it's often who you need. You fall quickly and you say so, which is lovely at the start. What partners find harder is that you show love by doing things. You fix the tap, you book the trip, you turn up with the car when it's raining. The long, slow talk about where the two of you are headed is another matter, and you can hear their wanting to have it as a complaint. It usually isn't one. Try staying in the chair a bit longer than feels comfortable.

You work best when there's something to win or something that doesn't exist yet. Launches, turnarounds, the first month of a new team, emergency work, sport, anything with a starting gun. The proposal nobody asked for, drafted and sent to the boss at nine on a Thursday night, is usually yours. Where it gets tricky is authority. A manager who hedges and says 'let's circle back' drives you mad, and you'll sometimes go around them, which works right up until it doesn't. You tend to do better under a blunt boss, even a harsh one, who makes decisions and lets you run. Plenty with this decan end up running their own show, partly so nobody can make them wait. Just be honest with yourself about who's going to do the invoicing.

At twenty this slice of Aries tends to be all launch. Three courses started, a band, a move interstate on a week's notice, and a fair few arguments you'd have won if you'd waited to hear the other half. That's normal, and plenty of it works out. By the mid-thirties most have lost something they didn't need to lose, a job walked out of in a temper or a friendship ended over something small, and the ones who do well learn to sleep on it before they act. They also pick a couple of things to carry the full distance, often a business, a family, or a skill they've kept at for a decade. By the fifties a lot of them become the person younger people ring when they need a push. They're still quick off the mark, they just choose their starts with more care.

Pick one thing you started in the last year and left half done. The course, the garden bed, the side project, the email to your cousin. Set a timer for twenty-five minutes and work only on the next piece of it, even if it's dull. When the timer goes, write the piece after that on a sticky note and put it where you'll see it in the morning. Do this on three separate days before you let yourself begin anything new.
